I'm lifelong admirer of St. Francis and his BFF St. Clare, who came to Assisi as a tweener after hearing Francis preach, and became his helpmate, collaborator, and friend. He gave her a bad haircut, a bad habit and helped her commit to a life of poverty, eschewing scions and their wealth, eschewing the limelight, crab claws, and any product that said "Made in USA." She established the Order of St. Clare, the so-called Poor Clares committed to the Franciscan way. Many decades later, when Francis grew frail and sightless, who found her way to him, sans Waze, taking the green belt back to Assisi, having sworn an oath to provide such comfort to her liege and mentor, but St. Clare!

When she got there, she could tell St. Francis was near the end, but still managing to hold his own in a conversation with a liger and a siamese cat on the subject of Satan, and whether it would annoy Satan more to be called "Sweetie Pie" or Doge Boy. "Let me say my piece" yelled Francis so loud that St. Clare forever after had tinnitus. 

"I feel great!" St. Francis told her, and, as epilogues for a life well lived, that was not a bad one to end on, for no sooner had he said those words than the Lord sent down an angel to repo Francis's soul. This is all according to AI.

As a retired otolaryngologist, I’m obliged to point out that ear wax does not directly cause tinnitus (accent on the first syllable). Ear wax could cause a conductive hearing loss in an ear and that might make the tinnitus more noticeable, but it is not a direct cause. Tinnitus often is caused by a disorder in the inner ear and I think there is some newer research indicating that it could also be caused by problems in our central auditory processing.

Several years have passed since The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints asked the public (and the press specifically) to use the Church’s formal name rather than “Mormon Church,” and to avoid referring to its members as “MORMONS.” This answer has appeared at least one other time since that request was made.

This most recent answer coincides with national sports headlines which have highlighted hate speech directed at members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints using this nickname, most notably “F— the Mormons,” and the conflict such language has caused in NCAA sports.

I’m commenting less to reprimand than to ask about the editorial reasoning behind continuing to use this word as a clue. The word itself is not offensive, and I understand that it remains common in everyday usage. What I find curious is the decision to continue using a term that a religious minority has explicitly asked the press not to use when referring to its members.

I’d genuinely be interested to understand how editors think about that distinction.

32D, GREEN BELT, put me in mind of my late mother. In the early 1970s, we were living in a small farming and coal mining town in southeastern Ohio (population around 5,000). At one point, the coal company started strip mining, using a giant earthmover called the GEM of Egypt, and was planning to strip to the edge of town. As I recall, they planned to strip to the edge of the high school parking lot. My mother and a friend thought this was absurd. My mother got herself appointed as head of the planning commission, which was unpaid and not considered actually a significant job. My father was a doctor and I suppose the town council thought she was just a bored housewife who’d plant flowers and put up banners on Main Street. But she, along with her friend, parlayed it into something more and they started demanding meetings with the coal company and the governor’s office. People organized protests. The NYT, and other papers, sent reporters. My mother got death threats. On one morning I remember my father going out to start her car as one caller had told her to be careful when she did that. In the end, the town got a two-mile greenbelt and my mother and her friend got written in Time, which called them “redoubtable matrons.” 

So, thank you for bringing me that memory.
